statement: Owen has an orange, a blue and a purple T-shirt, and black, white and grey shorts. He never wears orange with black. How many outfits of one T-shirt and shorts can he make?

choices.misconception: I took the orange T-shirt and the black shorts away completely, leaving 2 T-shirts and 2 shorts.
I added the 3 T-shirts and the 3 shorts instead of making pairs.
I took away the orange-with-black outfit twice, once for the T-shirt and once for the shorts.
I counted every outfit and forgot about the rule.

hints: Draw a tree: one branch for each T-shirt.
From each T-shirt, draw a branch for each pair of shorts. Count all the ends, then cross out any outfit the rule does not allow.
Each T-shirt goes with 3 shorts, so there are 3 x 3 outfits before the rule. The rule removes just one of them.

solutions.reliable: Each of the 3 T-shirts can go with each of the 3 shorts, which gives 9 outfits. The rule removes only orange with black, which is one outfit. That leaves 9 - 1 = 8. The idea to keep: count all the pairs first with a tree, then take away exactly the ones the rule forbids.
solutions.elegant: Count by T-shirt: orange goes with 2 shorts, blue with 3 and purple with 3, so 2 + 3 + 3 = 8.

whyOnTest: Tree diagrams make every pair visible, and a rule that removes one pair checks you do not remove too much.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
